SOURCE: "Adaptive Semiparametric Language Models" (SPALM), Dani Yogatama, Cyprien de Masson d'Autume, Lingpeng Kong (DeepMind). arXiv:2102.02557v1 [cs.CL], 4 Feb 2021. No venue is printed. The acknowledgements thank "the action editor (Mihai Surdeanu) and three anonymous reviewers" (p10), which points to a journal, consistent with TACL 2021. The PDF itself never names TACL, so cite it as arXiv 2102.02557 (2021) unless you confirm the TACL version separately.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/yogatama-2021-adaptive-semiparametric-language-models.pdf

COVERAGE: 47,654 of 47,654 chars read (11 pages), references included. The paper has no appendix. Figure captions come from figures.py.

IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: the paper has no Chinese Gigaword experiment. Its three datasets are WikiText-103, WMT (an English LM corpus the authors built from WMT 2019 news) and enwik8 (Table 1, p5). Do not put Chinese Gigaword into the note on this paper's authority.

CLAIMS
- claim: SPALM adds retrieval inside the LM architecture. It retrieves the k nearest-neighbour next tokens from a datastore that has one entry per training token, then a learned, context-dependent sigmoid gate mixes them with the transformer-XL hidden state before the softmax. kNN-LM instead interpolates at the output.
  number: one new parameter vector, w_g
  setup: architecture. Keys come from a separately pretrained vanilla transformer LM (final-layer hidden state) and are frozen. Values are next tokens, embedded with the base model's word embedding matrix.
  quote: "mt = sum_k softmax(y_k^T h_t^R) y_k ; gt = σ(w_g^T h_t^R) ; zt = (1− gt)⊙ mt + gt⊙ hRt" (equations reformatted from the extraction) and "given the database, the only additional parameter that needs to be trained is wg"
  where: p3
- claim: The paper's main argument against kNN-LM is that kNN-LM uses a single corpus-level λ tuned on a dev set, so it cannot adapt per token. SPALM's gate weights each token differently.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual comparison
  quote: "interpolating the language model weights at the corpus level forces the model to use the same interpolation weight λ for pLM and pkNN for each token in the corpus. It cannot adaptively combine short-term and long-term information at the token level"
  where: p4
- claim: On WikiText-103, SPALM alone does not beat kNN-LM on test perplexity. kNN-LM is marginally better on test, SPALM marginally better on dev. SPALM plus kNN interpolation gives the best result.
  number: M=512: TXL 19.6, kNN-LM 18.5, SPALM 18.8, SPALM+kNN 18.0 test ppl. M=3072: TXL 19.1, kNN-LM 18.0, SPALM 18.3, SPALM+kNN 17.6.
  setup: 18 layers, 512 hidden, 142M params, sequence length 512, k=4 neighbours, kNN-LM λ tuned from {0.05,...,0.4} on dev. In the same table, Khandelwal et al.'s own 247M kNN-LM reports 16.1 test.
  quote: "kNN-LM is marginally better on the test set even though SPALM is marginally better on the development set." / "resulting in the best model with a perplexity of 17.6." / Table 2 rows "kNN-LM 142M 17.7 18.0 / SPALM 142M 17.4 18.3 / ↪→ +kNN 17.2 17.6"

LIMITS
- Authors concede: neighbours must be retrieved for every training token, which is expensive (quote above). Keys are frozen and the model is not trained end to end ("we leave end-to-end training to future work", p4). Evaluation is static only, with no datastore growth and no comparison to dynamic evaluation (p4). Transformer-XL sometimes beats SPALM when a word already appeared in the extended context, because long-term memory "smoothed over" the distribution (p8). The Figure 2 example is "cherry-picked" (p7). The authors caution against drawing conclusions from the Figure 6 gate heatmap (p9).
- Not shown: no downstream tasks (QA, factuality, attribution), only perplexity and BPC. Models are small (100–148M). The datastore is the training corpus itself, so retrieval never reaches knowledge outside the training data. There is no scaling study, no inference-latency numbers, and no check for test/train overlap. On WikiText-103, SPALM alone loses to kNN-LM on test.
- Dated: these are 2021 small-model results. RETRO (2021/22) later scaled chunk-level retrieval into the LM, and its numbers are not comparable to these. Absolute ppl is worse than the published 247M kNN-LM (16.1).
- Embedded instructions: none found.

BUILDS ON: transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019) for short-term memory. kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020), its closest relative. Neural/continuous cache (Grave et al., 2017c) and pointer sentinel (Merity et al., 2017). The gate resembles Bapna and Firat (2019). ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020) for MIPS. Tied embeddings (Inan et al., 2017). Contrasted with REALM (Guu et al., 2020) and Megatron-CNTRL (Xu et al., 2020) as input-concatenation approaches. Also Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), adaptive softmax (Grave et al., 2017b) and kNN-MT (Khandelwal et al., 2021).

CODE: none in the paper. The gate equations quoted above (p3) are the core mechanism.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): "Our language model architecture has three main components: (i) a transformer that processes the current local context, (ii) a short-term memory module ..., (iii) and a key-value (hidden state-output token) database that stores compressed long-term context... We use a context-dependent gate to combine information from multiple sources". Best candidate for the note: one picture places retrieval inside the forward pass next to the KV cache, which contrasts directly with RAG's retrieval into the prompt. The extraction contains only latexit residue for the diagram, so check the rendered page.
- Fig 5 (p8): gate-value histograms, WMT vs enwik8. Second choice: it shows quickly that the model learns when to retrieve.

PROBLEMS: Figure 1 and Figure 6 diagram text came out as latexit base64 or scattered tokens. Captions and the table text extracted cleanly. The brief's Chinese Gigaword dataset does not appear anywhere in this paper. The venue is not printed (see SOURCE).
